title: When You Need To Be A Mean Teacher
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to a recurring question about whether SCM ever calls for confrontation or intimidation, Linsin gives an unequivocal answer: no. He argues that raising one's voice or showing anger may quell misbehavior momentarily through fear, but it always damages classroom management in the long run, regardless of grade level or student population. Negative methods create dislike and resentment that weaken accountability, since students who don't trust or enjoy being around a teacher stop caring about consequences; difficult and struggling students are hurt most, often regressing or shutting down. He also explains that emotional reactions shift responsibility from students back onto teachers, producing guilt-driven over-helping and inconsistency. The article closes by urging teachers to 'rise above,' framing taking misbehavior personally as both ineffective and, in his words, childish, and arguing that true leadership means holding oneself to a higher standard than the students.
points: Linsin states unequivocally that there is never a time a teacher needs to be confrontational, intimidating, or 'mean.'
Raising one's voice may suppress misbehavior briefly through fear, but always damages classroom management over the long term.
Negative methods create resentment that weakens a teacher's accountability system, since students who dislike a teacher stop caring about consequences.
Difficult students and those with learning or emotional difficulties are described as most negatively affected by negative teacher reactions.
Reacting emotionally to misbehavior shifts responsibility away from students and back onto the teacher, fueling guilt-driven over-helping and inconsistency.
quotes: There is never a time when you need to be confrontational or intimidating.
Although it’s true that raising your voice and getting angry can quell misbehavior in the moment—because of a natural fear response—it’s never good for the long-term health of your classroom.
You see, when your students don’t like you (often secretly), trust you, or enjoy being in your class, then your consequences won’t matter to them.

Difficult students, and students with learning, social, emotional, or attention difficulties, in particular, are the most negatively affected. They tend to regress, shut-down, and stop caring altogether rather than make any lasting improvement.
Taking misbehavior personally, becoming vengeful, and showing displeasure is not only ineffective and remarkably stressful. But it’s childish.
You must hold yourself to a higher standard. You must rise above and refuse to get dragged into arguments or succumb to hurt feelings and petty grievances.
